rows.question: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
queries: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of funds notice period demand payment
The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 section 138 notice demanding payment
The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 section 138 cause of action limitation period
rows.answer:
The notice period for making a demand for payment before filing a complaint is fifteen days from the date of receipt of the notice, as stated in Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1]. 

Conditions and time limits:
- The cheque must be presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier, according to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].
- The payee or holder in due course must make a demand for payment by giving a written notice to the drawer within thirty days of receiving information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid, under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].
- The drawer fails to make the payment within fifteen days of receiving the said notice, as set out in Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].

rows.question: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
queries: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
negotiable instrument presumption as to consideration holder in due course
Negotiable Instruments Act section 118 presumption as to consideration
Negotiable Instruments Act section 118 date stamp consideration transfer
rows.answer:
Every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration, under Section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1]. The court shall presume that the negotiable instrument was made for consideration, which throws the burden of proof of failure of consideration on the maker of the promissory note, as discussed in the Supreme Court judgment "K.P.O. Moideenkutty Hajee versus Pappu Manjooran and Anr." [11].

Related provisions:
- Section 43 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, covering negotiable instruments made, drawn, accepted, indorsed or transferred without consideration [3].
- Section 58 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, covering instruments obtained by unlawful means or for unlawful consideration [2].

rows.question: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
queries: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
contract voidable on account of coercion fraud misrepresentation
Indian Contract Act section 19 voidability of agreements without free consent
Indian Contract Act section 15 coercion defined and section 18 misrepresentation defined
rows.answer:
A contract can be avoided when consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud, or misrepresentation, making it a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused under Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. 

However, under the Exception to Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a contract caused by misrepresentation or by fraudulent silence is not voidable if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence [1].

I couldn't find any specific time limits or procedural conditions for avoiding such a contract in the Acts I searched.

rows.question: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
queries: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
topSources: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s7
rows.answer:
Every person who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, who is of sound mind, and who is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject, is competent to enter into a contract, as stated in Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. As discussed in the Supreme Court judgment in M/S N. N. Global Mercantile Private Limited versus M/S Indo Unique Flame Ltd. & Ors., Section 11 declares these criteria for contractual competence, while Section 12 articulates what constitutes a sound mind [12].

Related provisions:
- Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which covers what agreements are contracts, requiring them to be made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object [3].
- Section 7 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, which provides that every person competent to contract and entitled to transferable property, or authorised to dispose of transferable property not his own, is competent to transfer such property [4].

rows.question: What is the punishment for murder?
queries: What is the punishment for murder?
punishment for murder culpable homicide amounting to murder
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 103 punishment for murder
topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s531
rows.answer:
The punishment for murder is death or imprisonment for life, and liability to a fine under Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaced Section 300 and Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [1][4][10]. 

Related provisions:
- Section 104 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, covering punishment for murder by life-convict, which replaced Section 303 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [3].
- Section 101 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, covering the definition of murder, which replaced Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [4][10].
- Section 105 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, covering punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder, which replaced Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [2][9].
- Section 109 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, covering attempt to murder, which replaced Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [6].

rows.question: What is the punishment for theft?
queries: What is the punishment for theft?
punishment for theft Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 303 theft punishment
topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s2
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s359
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s531
rows.answer:
The punishment for theft is imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, and in case of a second or subsequent conviction, rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to five years and with fine, under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1] (which replaced section 379 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, as the current law). 

Conditions and time limits:
- In cases of theft where the value of the stolen property is less than five thousand rupees, and a person is convicted for the first time, upon return of the value of the property or restoration of the stolen property, the person shall be punished with community service under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 305 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers theft in a dwelling house, or means of transportation or place of worship, etc., with imprisonment up to seven years and fine [5].
- Section 306 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers theft by a clerk or servant of property in possession of a master, with imprisonment up to seven years and fine [7].

rows.question: When can a person accused of a non-bailable offence be released on bail?

rows.answer:
A person accused or suspected of a non-bailable offence may be released on bail by an officer in charge of a police station or a court other than the High Court or Court of Session, except where there appear reasonable grounds for believing the person has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, or is a cognizable offender with prior convictions for offences punishable with death, imprisonment for life, imprisonment for seven years or more, or two or more prior convictions for cognizable offences carrying three to seven years of imprisonment [1]. The Supreme Court, discussing the parallel provision under Section 437(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (which has been replaced by Section 480 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023), observed that a ban is imposed against granting bail if there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, but in all other non-bailable cases judicial discretion is exercised in favour of granting bail subject to conditions [11][12].

queries: On what grounds can an arbitral award be set aside and within what time?

rows.answer:
An arbitral award may be set aside by the Court only on the grounds specified in sub-section (2) and sub-section (2A) of Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 [1]. 

The grounds on which an arbitral award may be set aside are:
- A party was under some incapacity [1][12][13].
- The arbitration agreement is not valid under the law to which the parties have subjected it or, failing any indication thereon, under the law for the time being in force [1][12][13].
- The party making the application was not given proper notice of the appointment of an arbitrator or of the arbitral proceedings or was otherwise unable to present his case [1][12][13].
- The arbitral award deals with a dispute not contemplated by or not falling within the terms of the submission to arbitration, or it contains decisions on matters beyond the scope of the submission to arbitration, provided that if decisions on matters submitted can be separated from those not submitted, only the part containing decisions on matters not submitted may be set aside [1][12][13].

rows.question: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
queries: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
sale of immovable property definition transfer of ownership price paid or promised
Transfer of Property Act 1882 section 54 sale how made delivery of tangible immovable property
Transfer of Property Act 1882 contract for sale rights and liabilities of buyer and seller
topSources: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s54
The Sale of Goods Act, 1930 s4
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s55
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s58
rows.answer:
A sale of immovable property is defined as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1].

As discussed in the Supreme Court judgment Lucknow Nagar Nigam & Others versus Kohli Brothers Colour Lab. Pvt. Ltd. & Others, in order to constitute a sale, there must be a transfer of ownership from one person to another, meaning all rights and interests possessed by a person are transferred with free consent for a price called consideration, the conveyance has to be regarded in accordance with law, and the transferor cannot retain any part of their interest or right [11].

Conditions and time limits:
- In the case of tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, or a reversion or other intangible thing, the transfer can be made only by a registered instrument under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1].

rows.question: What are the inherent powers of a civil court?
queries: What are the inherent powers of a civil court?
inherent powers of court savings of inherent powers of civil court
Code of Civil Procedure section 151
topSources: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 s151
The Metro Railways (Construction of Works) Act, 1978 s16B

rows.answer:
Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 states that nothing in the Code shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect the inherent power of the Court to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of the Court [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 16B of The Metro Railways (Construction of Works) Act, 1978, which provides that the competent authority and the appellate authority may exercise powers of the nature referred to in section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 to the same extent and for the same purposes as such civil court powers [2].
- Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which is the current law (in force from 1 July 2024) replacing Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (the old law) regarding the saving of inherent powers of the High Court [3][13]. The text of the old Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is not in our data yet.
